findings.title: Nonhispanic pct grim impossible
findings.description: n=618 is a STATED denominator, not an assumed one: the paper says 618 mothers were interviewed at child age 18 y, the arm split 192+426=618 reconciles exactly, and the three race counts 5+578+35 sum to exactly 618. No integer count out of 618 yields 98.8%. The printed count 617 gives 617/618 = 99.8%, which IS attainable. This is therefore an isolated typographical error (99.8 mis-set as 98.8), not a data-integrity problem: the companion percentages 0.8/93.5/5.7 all pass GRIM at n=618. Flagged `impossible` because the printed value violates arithmetic as written, but the benign explanation is strongly supported.

findings.title: Intergenerational correlation out of range (Results, Intergenerational Mobility, para 1)
findings.description: A correlation coefficient of 11.3 is definitionally impossible. The companion figure in the same sentence -- a 0.188 treatment difference in the SAME intergenerational correlation coefficients -- is internally inconsistent with 11.3 by a factor of ~60, but is fully consistent with a control-group correlation of 0.113. The overwhelmingly likely explanation is a decimal/typesetting error (0.113 printed as 11.3), not a data problem. Recorded as impossible-as-printed; the substantive point is that the number as published cannot be interpreted and the underlying analysis lives in eTable 8 of an unavailable supplement.

findings.title: Mht p smaller than uncorrected p (Tables 1, 3 and 4, 'MHT P value' vs 'P value' columns)
findings.description: Seven rows print a Romano-Wolf multiplicity-corrected p BELOW the uncorrected p. Small reversals are legitimate under bootstrap stepdown, so this is not by itself an error. The one that warrants clarification is Table 4, Maternal stage 1 hypertension at 12 y, Mothers of females: raw P = .01 corrected to MHT P = '.00'. A p-value printed as .00 is uninformative and, read literally, states p = 0. The analogous 12-and-18-y row in the same table prints .002, so the precision convention is inconsistent within a single column.

findings.title: Debit binary proportions indeterminate
findings.description: IMPORTANT NEGATIVE RESULT. DEBIT is the natural check here -- every outcome is a 0/1 indicator whose SD is fully determined by its mean and n -- but the paper never reports per-arm sample sizes, only a combined row N. An initial batch run using arm sizes inferred from the 228:514 allocation returned 3 'impossible' rows. Every one of those three REVERSES to consistent at a different plausible n: 0.31 (0.47) is impossible at n=212 but consistent at n=207 and n=400; 0.02 (0.16) is consistent at n=80 and n=120; 0.05 (0.23) is consistent at n=110. The three flags were artefacts of my own assumed denominators, not properties of the data, and are withdrawn. Per rulebook rule 4 no DEBIT verdict on t

findings.notes: Produced by absence_of_evidence (CLI verb: absence-of-evidence); technique recorded as `manual` because the schema enum has no absence_of_evidence entry. The paper's null claims are stated flatly ('no effect', 'No intervention effect was found') in the Abstract, Key Points and Conclusions, but the underlying intervals are wide enough to be compatible with substantial effects -- up to a 6.4-fold difference for female offspring stage 1 hypertension and a 2.2-fold INCREASE for male offspring obesity. The male-obesity interval (0.963-2.197) is in fact directionally adverse and borderline. Because the paper states no smallest effect size of interest, the tool correctly declines to judge equivalence, and that refusal is the recorded result. The asymmetry matters editorially: the same evidential standard is not applied to the positive female findings and the null male findings.

findings.title: Headline effect size plausibility
findings.description: Produced by check_effect_plausibility (CLI verb: effect-size). Guards against a false positive. An 81% relative risk reduction sounds extraordinary, but on the standardised scale it is d = 0.35, squarely at the medicine_rct median of 0.3 -- because a large RELATIVE reduction on a rare binary outcome (12% vs 2%) is a modest ABSOLUTE and standardised effect. The headline effect magnitude is therefore NOT implausible and should not be flagged as too-good-to-be-true. Caveat: per-arm ns were inferred from the 228:514 allocation, though d is nearly insensitive to them; and d benchmarks are calibrated on continuous outcomes, so this is an approximate comparison.
